specStatements.text: Students should be able to explain how the power transfer in any circuit device is related to the potential difference across it and the current through it, and to the energy changes over time:
power = potential difference × current
[P = V I]
power = (current)^2 × resistance
power, P, in watts, W
potential difference, V, in volts, V
current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere)
resistance, R, in ohms, Ω
Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers.
The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on how long the appliance is switched on for and the power of the appliance.
Students should be able to describe how different domestic appliances transfer energy from batteries or ac mains to the kinetic energy of electric motors or the energy of heating devices.
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit.
The amount of energy transferred by electrical work can be calculated using the equation:
energy transferred = power × time
[E = P t]
energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference
[E = Q V]
energy transferred, E, in joules, J
power, P, in watts, W
time, t, in seconds, s
charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C
potential difference, V, in volts, V
Students should be able to explain how the power of a circuit device is related to:
• the potential difference across it and the current through it
• the energy transferred over a given time.
Students should be able to describe, with examples, the relationship between the power ratings for domestic electrical appliances and the changes in stored energy when they are in use.
The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
Electrical power is transferred from power stations to consumers using the National Grid.

Step-up transformers are used to increase the potential difference from the power station to the transmission cables then step-down transformers are used to decrease, to a much lower value, the potential difference for domestic use.
Students should be able to explain why the National Grid system is an efficient way to transfer energy.

concepts.term: Power transfer in a circuit device
concepts.definition: The power of a circuit device is the energy it transfers each second. A device with a larger power transfers more energy in the same time. Power is measured in watts, W, and 1 W is a transfer of 1 J each second.

concepts.term: power = potential difference × current (P = V I)
concepts.definition: The power transfer in any circuit device equals the potential difference across it multiplied by the current through it: P = V I, with P in watts, W, V in volts, V, and I in amperes, A. This equation must be recalled and applied.

The power transfer in a device can also be found from the current through it and its resistance: P = I² R, with P in watts, W, I in amperes, A, and R in ohms, Ω. Because the current is squared, doubling the current gives four times the power.
The quantity symbol for potential difference is V and it is measured in volts, whose unit symbol is also V. It is the quantity that appears in P = V I and in E = Q V.
The quantity symbol for current is I and it is measured in amperes, A. The word amp is acceptable in place of ampere.
The quantity symbol for resistance is R and it is measured in ohms, whose unit symbol is Ω. Resistance appears in the power equation P = I² R.
The watt is the unit of power, with unit symbol W. Because power is energy transferred per second, a power of 1 W means 1 joule is transferred every second.

concepts.term: Appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers
concepts.definition: Everyday electrical appliances are built so that the electrical work done on them produces a particular useful energy transfer, for example turning a motor or heating water. The design of the appliance decides which transfer happens.

concepts.term: What the energy transferred depends on
concepts.definition: The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on two things: how long the appliance is switched on for, and the power of the appliance. Neither one alone decides the total energy transferred.
In appliances such as a food mixer, an electric drill or a washing machine drum, energy is transferred electrically from the battery or the ac mains to the kinetic energy store of the rotating motor.

In appliances such as a kettle, a toaster or an electric heater, energy is transferred electrically from the battery or the ac mains to the thermal energy store of the heating element and of whatever it heats.

concepts.term: Batteries and ac mains as supplies
concepts.definition: Domestic appliances are supplied either by batteries, which provide a direct current, or by the ac mains, which provides an alternating current. Either supply can do electrical work on the appliance and bring about the same kind of energy transfer.
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit. The power supply does work pushing charge through the components, and that work is the energy transferred electrically to the components.

concepts.term: energy transferred = power × time (E = P t)
concepts.definition: The energy transferred by electrical work equals the power of the device multiplied by the time it operates: E = P t, with E in joules, J, P in watts, W, and t in seconds, s. The time must be converted to seconds before use.

concepts.term: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference (E = Q V)
concepts.definition: The energy transferred by electrical work also equals the charge that flows multiplied by the potential difference it moves through: E = Q V, with E in joules, J, Q in coulombs, C, and V in volts, V.
The joule is the unit of energy transferred, with unit symbol J. Both E = P t and E = Q V give the energy transferred in joules when the other quantities are in their own standard units.
The quantity symbol for time is t and it is measured in seconds, s. A time given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before it is substituted into E = P t.
The quantity symbol for charge flow is Q and it is measured in coulombs, C. Charge flow is the amount of charge that passes a point, not the rate at which it passes, which is the current.

concepts.term: Power rating of a domestic appliance
concepts.definition: The power rating printed on an appliance states the power in watts it transfers when in normal use. A higher power rating means a faster change in stored energy: a 2000 W kettle empties the mains supply of energy and fills the water's thermal store far faster than a 60 W lamp fills its surroundings.
The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers. It is the network through which electrical power reaches homes, schools and factories.
A step-up transformer is used to increase the potential difference from the power station to the transmission cables, so that the same power can be transferred with a much smaller current.
A step-down transformer is used to decrease the potential difference, to a much lower value, for domestic use. It sits between the transmission cables and the consumer.

concepts.term: Why the National Grid is efficient
concepts.definition: For a given power, P = V I means that raising the potential difference lowers the current in the transmission cables. The power wasted heating the cables is given by P = I² R, so a smaller current wastes far less energy. Transformers therefore make the grid an efficient way to transfer energy over long distances.
Electrical power is transferred from power stations to consumers using the National Grid. The grid transfers the power that power stations generate; it does not generate or store it.

concepts.term: Linking power, potential difference, current and energy over time
concepts.definition: The power of a circuit device is set by the potential difference across it and the current through it (P = V I), and it is also the energy transferred over a given time (E = P t, so P = E ÷ t). The two routes must give the same power for the same device.

misconceptions.question: A kettle is labelled 2000 W. How much energy does it transfer?
misconceptions.correct: The label gives the power, not the energy. The energy transferred also depends on the time: E = P t, so 2000 W for 90 s transfers 180 000 J.
misconceptions.misconception: The number on the label is the energy, so a 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power and energy are both 'how much' quantities in everyday speech, and the label is the only number the student is given.
misconceptions.correction: Read the watt as 'joules every second'. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J each second, so you must multiply by the number of seconds to get the energy.

misconceptions.question: Appliance A is rated 1200 W and appliance B is rated 400 W. Which transfers more energy?
misconceptions.correct: You cannot tell without the times. Energy transferred depends on both the power and how long the appliance is switched on for.
misconceptions.misconception: The one with the bigger power rating always transfers more energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power rating is the number students are shown most often, so it becomes the only variable they attend to.
misconceptions.correction: Always compute E = P t for each appliance. A 400 W appliance run for 20 minutes transfers more energy than a 1200 W appliance run for 5 minutes.

misconceptions.question: What kind of store does a mains-powered kettle draw energy from?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is transferred electrically from the mains supply to the thermal store of the water; the mains itself is not described as a chemical store.
misconceptions.misconception: The mains supply is a chemical store of energy, just like a battery.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Batteries are introduced first and do involve chemical stores, so students generalise the idea to every electrical supply.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the pathway, not the socket: energy is transferred electrically from the supply to the store in the appliance. Only the battery itself holds a chemical store.

misconceptions.question: The potential difference across a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to its power?
misconceptions.correct: The current also doubles, so from P = V I the power becomes four times as large.
misconceptions.misconception: Power is proportional to potential difference, so doubling the pd doubles the power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read P = V I as if only V changes, holding I fixed, because I is a separate symbol on the page.
misconceptions.correction: Check whether the other quantity changes too. For a fixed resistance, doubling V doubles I, so P = V I gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the power.

misconceptions.question: Does the power of a fixed resistor change if the supply is changed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Resistance is fixed, but the current and potential difference change, so the power changes.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the resistance of the resistor does not change, its power cannot change either.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat every property printed on a component as a fixed characteristic of that component, including the power.
misconceptions.correction: Resistance is a property of the component; power depends on how hard the circuit drives it, through P = V I or P = I² R.

misconceptions.question: A lamp has 12 V across it and 2.5 A through it. What is the power?
misconceptions.misconception: To get power you divide the potential difference by the current, giving 4.8 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The most-practised electrical equation is V = I R, which is usually rearranged by dividing, so dividing becomes the default move.
misconceptions.correction: P = V I is a product, not a ratio. Dividing V by I would give the resistance in ohms, not a power in watts.

misconceptions.question: In P = V I, does anything need squaring?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only P = I² R contains a square, and it is the current that is squared.
misconceptions.misconception: You square the current in P = V I as well, so 12 V and 2.5 A give 12 × 2.5² = 75 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two power equations are learned together and the square migrates from one to the other.
misconceptions.correction: Match the equation to the quantities you are given: pd and current means P = V I with no square; current and resistance means P = I² R with the current squared.

misconceptions.question: A 5.0 Ω resistor carries 3.0 A. What is the power?
misconceptions.misconception: The square can be dropped, so P = I R = 3.0 × 5.0 = 15 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 15 W is what V = I R produces, and the familiar shape of that equation overwrites the unfamiliar squared term.
misconceptions.correction: I R gives a potential difference in volts, not a power in watts. Square the current first, then multiply by the resistance.

misconceptions.question: In P = I² R, which quantity is squared?
misconceptions.correct: The current is squared. The resistance is not.
misconceptions.misconception: The resistance is squared, so a 3.0 A current in a 5.0 Ω resistor gives 3.0 × 5.0² = 75 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The superscript is read as belonging to the whole right-hand side rather than to the symbol it sits on.
misconceptions.correction: The index sits on I alone. Write the substitution as (3.0)² × 5.0 so the square is unmistakably attached to the current.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the charge as it flows round a circuit?
misconceptions.correct: The charge is not used up; it keeps flowing round. What is transferred away from the supply is energy, and work is done as the charge flows.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge gets used up by the components as it goes round the circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Batteries do go flat, and students attach that running-out to the charge rather than to the energy stored chemically.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two ideas: the same charge circulates continuously, while energy is transferred from the supply to the components as work is done.

misconceptions.question: Is work done in a circuit even though nothing visibly moves?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Work is done when charge flows in a circuit, and that work is the energy transferred electrically.
misconceptions.misconception: Work is only done when an object moves, so no work is done in a circuit with no moving parts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work is first met as force × distance with a visibly moving object, so an invisible flow of charge does not look like work.
misconceptions.correction: Charge moving through a potential difference is movement. The supply does work on the charge, which is why E = Q V gives an energy in joules.

misconceptions.question: A 2000 W heater is on for 3 minutes. How much energy is transferred?
misconceptions.correct: Convert to seconds first: t = 180 s, so E = P t = 2000 × 180 = 360 000 J.
misconceptions.misconception: The time can be substituted as it is given, so E = 2000 × 3 = 6000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The question states the time in minutes, and students substitute the number they are shown without checking the unit.
misconceptions.correction: In E = P t, t must be in seconds, s. Convert minutes and hours to seconds before substituting.

misconceptions.question: How do you combine power and time to find energy?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply them: energy transferred = power × time, E = P t.
misconceptions.misconception: You divide the power by the time, so 2000 W over 180 s gives about 11 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power is often described as 'energy per second', and the word per makes students divide by the time instead of multiplying.
misconceptions.correction: Power per second means energy each second, so multiply by the number of seconds. Dividing gives a quantity with no physical meaning here.

misconceptions.question: In E = Q V, what does Q stand for?
misconceptions.correct: Q is the charge flow, measured in coulombs, C.
misconceptions.misconception: Q is the current, so you can put the number of amperes straight into E = Q V.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Current and charge are both about 'electricity moving', and Q appears in Q = I t alongside current.
misconceptions.correction: Charge flow is in coulombs; current is in amperes. If you are given a current and a time, first find Q = I t, then use E = Q V.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of energy transferred?
misconceptions.correct: Energy transferred, E, is measured in joules, J. Power, P, is measured in watts, W.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy is measured in watts, because appliances are labelled in watts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only electrical unit students meet on real appliances is the watt, so it becomes their default energy unit.
misconceptions.correction: The watt measures the rate of transfer. The answer to any E = P t or E = Q V calculation is in joules.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of current?
misconceptions.correct: Current, I, is measured in amperes, A; amp is acceptable for ampere. Coulombs measure charge flow.
misconceptions.misconception: Current is measured in coulombs, because current is about charge moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are introduced together and both are described using the word charge.
misconceptions.correction: One ampere is one coulomb passing each second. The coulomb measures how much charge; the ampere measures how fast it passes.

misconceptions.question: A charge of 300 C flows through a lamp. Is 300 J transferred?
misconceptions.correct: No. The energy also depends on the potential difference: E = Q V, so at 12 V the transfer is 3600 J.
misconceptions.misconception: The charge flow is the energy transferred, so 300 C means 300 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are single numbers describing 'how much has gone through', so students treat them as the same quantity in different clothes.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is what flows; energy is what the charge delivers. Multiply the charge by the potential difference it moves through.

misconceptions.question: 540 J is transferred when 45 C flows through a lamp. What is the pd?
misconceptions.correct: Rearrange E = Q V to give V = E ÷ Q = 540 ÷ 45 = 12 V.
misconceptions.misconception: You multiply the energy by the charge, giving 540 × 45 = 24 300 V.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recall that the equation involves a product and multiply the two numbers they are given without rearranging first.
misconceptions.correction: Write the equation, identify which symbol is unknown, then rearrange. Only the two quantities on the right are multiplied together.

misconceptions.question: How does an electric motor in a food mixer receive its energy?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is transferred electrically from the supply to the kinetic energy store of the rotating motor.
misconceptions.misconception: The motor is driven by heating, because the current makes the wires hot and the heat makes it turn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know current warms wires, so heating becomes the mechanism they reach for in every electrical device.
misconceptions.correction: Name the pathway correctly: the transfer to a motor is electrical, and the useful store filled is kinetic. Heating in the wires is a wasteful side effect.

misconceptions.question: Does a battery supply ac or dc, and what about the mains?
misconceptions.correct: A battery supplies direct current; the mains supplies alternating current, which is why the specification says 'ac mains'.
misconceptions.misconception: Batteries give ac because the charge keeps moving, and the mains gives dc because it is steady.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words alternating and direct are not connected to anything the student can see, so the labels get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Link 'ac' to the mains socket and 'dc' to the battery. Both can drive the same appliance and bring about the same energy transfer.

misconceptions.question: Do battery-powered appliances transfer energy in the same way as mains ones?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A cordless drill and a mains drill both transfer energy electrically to the kinetic store of the motor.
misconceptions.misconception: Only mains appliances transfer energy electrically; battery ones work in some other way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mains appliances are described using the word electricity far more often, so the battery route feels like a different phenomenon.
misconceptions.correction: The supply differs, the transfer does not. In both cases the supply does electrical work on the charge flowing through the motor.

misconceptions.question: A transmission cable carries 100 A and has a resistance of 4.0 Ω. What power is wasted?
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply the current by the resistance: 100 × 4.0 = 400 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pattern 'current times resistance' is heavily practised through V = I R and is applied here without checking the equation.
misconceptions.correction: For wasted power use P = I² R and square the current first. The answer 400 would be a potential difference in volts.

misconceptions.question: The current in a cable is reduced to one tenth. What happens to the power wasted?
misconceptions.correct: Power wasted falls to one hundredth, because P = I² R depends on the square of the current.
misconceptions.misconception: The power wasted also falls to one tenth, because power and current go together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume proportionality by default and do not notice that the square changes the scaling factor.
misconceptions.correction: Scale the squared quantity: (1/10)² = 1/100. Halving the current quarters the wasted power, and so on.

misconceptions.question: Where are step-up and step-down transformers placed in the National Grid?
misconceptions.correct: Step-up transformers raise the pd from the power station to the transmission cables; step-down transformers lower it, to a much lower value, for domestic use.
misconceptions.misconception: Step-down transformers are at the power station and step-up transformers are near homes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'up' with going up the pylons towards the house at the end of the journey, rather than with the potential difference.
misconceptions.correction: The words describe the potential difference, not position or direction of travel. Homes need a much lower pd, so the last transformer must step down.

misconceptions.question: Why is a high potential difference used in the transmission cables?
misconceptions.correct: For a given power, a higher pd means a smaller current, and a smaller current wastes far less energy heating the cables.
misconceptions.misconception: The transformers increase the current so that more power can be pushed through to consumers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bigger is assumed to be better for everything, and current is the quantity students most associate with 'how much electricity'.
misconceptions.correction: P = V I: at fixed power, raising V must lower I. The saving comes from the smaller current, through P = I² R.

misconceptions.question: Does raising the potential difference change the resistance of the cables?
misconceptions.correct: No. The cable resistance is unchanged; it is the current that falls, and the wasted power falls with the square of the current.
misconceptions.misconception: A high potential difference lowers the resistance of the transmission cables, so less energy is wasted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know less energy is wasted and reach for resistance as the only obvious cause, since resistance is what wastes energy.
misconceptions.correction: Resistance depends on the cable itself, not on the supply. Identify the quantity that actually changes, which is the current.

misconceptions.question: Do transformers make up for the energy wasted in the cables?
misconceptions.correct: No. Transformers change the potential difference; they do not create energy. They reduce the waste by allowing a smaller current.
misconceptions.misconception: Transformers add extra energy back into the system to replace what the cables waste.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Step-up sounds like a boost, and students picture the transformer topping the supply back up.
misconceptions.correction: A transformer changes potential difference and current together, keeping the power transferred essentially the same. Energy is never added.

misconceptions.question: What does the National Grid actually do?
misconceptions.correct: It is a system of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers and transfers electrical power between them.
misconceptions.misconception: The National Grid is where the country's electricity is generated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: News reports talk about the grid supplying the country, which sounds like the grid is the source.
misconceptions.correction: Power stations generate; the grid transfers. The grid's parts are cables and transformers, not generators.

misconceptions.question: Does the National Grid store electricity until consumers need it?
misconceptions.correct: No. The grid transfers electrical power from power stations to consumers; it is a transfer system, not a store.
misconceptions.misconception: Electricity is stored in the grid's cables, like water in a reservoir, and drawn out when an appliance is switched on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word grid suggests a reservoir or supply, and taps and reservoirs are the everyday model for anything piped to a house.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the grid as cables and transformers that carry power as it is generated, so demand must be matched by generation at the time.

misconceptions.question: Two appliances are switched on for the same time. Do they transfer the same energy?
misconceptions.correct: Only if their powers are equal. In one minute a 900 W microwave transfers 54 000 J while a 60 W lamp transfers 3600 J.
misconceptions.misconception: If two appliances run for the same length of time they must transfer the same amount of energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Once the times match, students see only one variable left and assume the outcome must match too.
misconceptions.correction: Energy depends on the power as well as the time. Work out E = P t for each appliance separately and compare.

misconceptions.question: Does the energy transferred depend only on how long an appliance is on?
misconceptions.correct: No. It depends on how long the appliance is switched on for and on the power of the appliance.
misconceptions.misconception: The longer it is on, the more energy it transfers, so time alone decides the energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Time is the variable students can see changing, and 'leaving things on' is the everyday message about wasting energy.
misconceptions.correction: Both factors matter. Halving the power and doubling the time leaves the energy transferred unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Should the potential difference be stepped up everywhere in the National Grid?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is stepped up onto the transmission cables, then stepped down to a much lower value for domestic use.
misconceptions.misconception: Since a high potential difference is efficient, every transformer in the grid must step it up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that a high pd reduces waste and apply that rule to the whole journey, without asking what pd a house actually needs.
misconceptions.correction: The high pd is only useful in the long transmission cables. Consumers need a much lower value, so the last transformer must step down.

misconceptions.question: To find V from E = Q V, does it matter which way round you divide?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. V = E ÷ Q, so 540 J ÷ 45 C = 12 V. Dividing the other way gives 0.083, which is not a potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: As long as you divide the two numbers given, you will get the right answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that a division is needed but rearrange by feel rather than by algebra, often dividing the smaller number by the larger.
misconceptions.correction: Rearrange the equation on paper first, then substitute. Checking units helps: joules ÷ coulombs gives volts, coulombs ÷ joules does not.

mcqs.stem: A lamp has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 2.5 A through it. What is the power transfer in the lamp?

options.rationale: 12 ÷ 2.5, from treating the power equation as a division in the way V = I R is usually rearranged.
P = V I = 12 × 2.5 = 30 W, with pd in volts and current in amperes giving power in watts.
12 × 2.5², from carrying the square in P = I² R across into P = V I.
12 + 2.5, from adding the two given values when the operation is not recalled.

mcqs.stem: A current of 3.0 A passes through a resistor of resistance 5.0 Ω. What is the power transfer in the resistor?

options.rationale: 3.0 × 5.0, from dropping the square; this is in fact the potential difference in volts.
3.0 × 5.0², from squaring the resistance instead of the current.
3.0 ÷ 5.0, from dividing the two given values rather than using the stated equation.

mcqs.stem: Which row gives the correct unit for every quantity in the equation P = I² R?

options.text: power in watts, current in amperes, resistance in ohms
options.rationale: These are the units the specification states for P, I and R.

options.text: power in joules, current in amperes, resistance in ohms
options.rationale: The joule is the unit of energy transferred, not of power; power is a rate.

options.text: power in watts, current in coulombs, resistance in ohms
options.rationale: The coulomb is the unit of charge flow; current is measured in amperes.

options.text: power in watts, current in amperes, resistance in volts
options.rationale: The volt is the unit of potential difference; resistance is measured in ohms.

mcqs.stem: The potential difference across a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to the power transfer in the resistor?

options.text: The power becomes exactly twice as large
options.rationale: Chosen by treating I in P = V I as if it stayed fixed when the pd was doubled.

options.text: The power stays exactly the same value
options.rationale: Chosen because the resistance is unchanged, mistaking a component property for the power.

options.text: The power becomes four times larger
options.rationale: Doubling V also doubles I in a fixed resistance, so P = V I gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the power.

options.text: The power becomes half of its old value
options.rationale: Chosen by reasoning that a larger pd must be shared out, so each part receives less power.

mcqs.stem: The specification states that work is done when charge flows in a circuit. What does this mean?

options.text: Charge is gradually used up as it goes round the circuit
options.rationale: Chosen because batteries go flat; it is energy that is transferred away, not charge that is consumed.

options.text: Energy is transferred as charge is pushed through the components
options.rationale: The supply does work on the charge, and that work is the energy transferred electrically.

options.text: Work is done only when part of the circuit actually moves
options.rationale: Chosen from the force × distance definition of work met with visibly moving objects.

options.text: Current is transferred from the battery to the components
options.rationale: Chosen by treating current as a substance that leaves the supply and is delivered to components.

mcqs.stem: An electric heater has a power of 2000 W and is switched on for 3.0 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?

options.rationale: 2000 × 3, from substituting the time in minutes instead of converting it to seconds.
2000 ÷ 3, from reading 'energy per second' as an instruction to divide by the time.
2000 × 60, from converting only one minute to seconds and ignoring the factor of 3.

mcqs.stem: A current of 0.50 A flows for 600 s through a component with a potential difference of 12 V across it. How much energy is transferred?

options.rationale: 0.50 × 12 is the power in watts, quoted as though it were the energy transferred.
The charge flow of 300 C reported as an energy, treating charge and energy as the same quantity.
12 × 600, from multiplying the pd by the time and leaving the current out entirely.

mcqs.stem: Which row gives the correct unit for every quantity in the equation E = Q V?

options.text: E in joules, Q in amperes, V in volts
options.rationale: Chosen by reading Q as the current; charge flow is measured in coulombs.

options.text: E in watts, Q in coulombs, V in volts
options.rationale: Chosen because appliances are labelled in watts; the watt measures power, not energy.

options.text: E in joules, Q in coulombs, V in volts
options.rationale: These are the units the specification states for energy transferred, charge flow and potential difference.

options.text: E in joules, Q in coulombs, V in ohms
options.rationale: Chosen by confusing potential difference with resistance, which is the quantity measured in ohms.

mcqs.stem: A food mixer is plugged into the ac mains and switched on. Which statement best describes the useful energy transfer?

options.text: Energy is transferred electrically to a chemical energy store
options.rationale: Chosen by carrying the chemical store of a battery over to the appliance being driven.

options.text: Energy is transferred electrically to a kinetic energy store
options.rationale: The mains does electrical work on the motor, filling the kinetic store of the rotating blades.

options.text: Energy is transferred by heating to a kinetic energy store
options.rationale: Chosen because current warms wires, so heating is assumed to be the driving pathway.

options.text: Energy is transferred from a kinetic store to the mains supply
options.rationale: Chosen by reversing the direction of transfer between supply and appliance.

mcqs.stem: A cordless drill runs from a rechargeable battery. An identical mains drill runs from the ac mains. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the mains drill transfers energy electrically to a motor
options.rationale: Chosen because mains appliances are the ones usually described as electrical.

options.text: The battery drill uses ac and the mains drill uses dc supply
options.rationale: The labels are swapped: a battery supplies dc and the mains supplies ac.

options.text: Only the battery drill can transfer energy to a kinetic store
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming the portable device must work by a different mechanism from a wired one.

options.text: Both drills transfer energy electrically to a kinetic store
options.rationale: Battery and ac mains supplies both do electrical work on the motor, filling its kinetic energy store.

mcqs.stem: Appliance A has a power of 1200 W and is used for 5.0 minutes. Appliance B has a power of 400 W and is used for 20 minutes. Which transfers more energy?

options.text: A, because its power rating is three times that of B
options.rationale: Chosen by comparing power ratings alone and ignoring the times.

options.text: B, because time alone decides the energy transferred
options.rationale: Chosen by comparing only the times; A has three times the power, so the powers must be used too.

options.text: B, because it transfers 480 000 J and A only 360 000 J
Neither, because both are used at the same mains voltage
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming a shared supply voltage fixes the energy transferred.

mcqs.stem: A 900 W microwave oven and a 60 W lamp are each switched on for exactly 1.0 minute. Which statement about the energy transferred is correct?

options.text: The microwave transfers 900 J and the lamp only 60 J
options.rationale: The power rating is quoted as the energy, ignoring the 60 seconds of operation.

options.text: The microwave transfers 54 000 W and the lamp 3600 W
options.rationale: Correct numbers with the wrong unit: E = P t gives an energy in joules, not watts.

options.text: Both transfer the same energy because the times are equal
options.rationale: Chosen by treating equal times as enough to make the energy transfers equal.

options.text: The microwave transfers 54 000 J and the lamp 3600 J
options.rationale: E = P t with t = 60 s gives 900 × 60 = 54 000 J and 60 × 60 = 3600 J.

mcqs.stem: What is the National Grid?

options.text: A system of power stations that generates all of the country's electricity
options.rationale: Chosen by confusing the transfer network with the power stations that generate.

options.text: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers
options.rationale: This is the definition given in the specification.

options.text: A network of cables that stores electricity until consumers need it
options.rationale: Chosen by modelling the grid as a reservoir that is drawn from on demand.

options.text: A set of step-up transformers that supply homes with electricity
options.rationale: Chosen by remembering transformers but keeping only the step-up ones and dropping the cables.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes where the transformers are used in the National Grid?

options.text: Step-down transformers near power stations, step-up near homes
options.rationale: The two are swapped, usually by linking 'up' to the journey towards homes rather than to the pd.

options.text: Step-up transformers at both ends of the transmission cables
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming a high potential difference is wanted all the way to the consumer.

options.text: Step-down transformers at both ends of the transmission cables
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming the pd must be lowered for safety immediately at the power station.

options.text: Step-up transformers near power stations, step-down near consumers
options.rationale: Step-up transformers raise the pd onto the transmission cables; step-down transformers lower it for domestic use.

mcqs.stem: Why does transferring electrical power at a very high potential difference make the National Grid an efficient way to transfer energy?

options.text: The current is smaller, so less energy is wasted heating the cables
options.rationale: P = V I means a higher pd needs a smaller current for the same power, and P = I² R then gives a much smaller wasted power.

options.text: The current is larger, so more energy reaches the consumers quickly
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming a bigger current means more electricity delivered.

options.text: The resistance of the cables is reduced by the high potential difference
options.rationale: Resistance is a property of the cable and is not changed by the supply.

options.text: The transformers add extra energy to replace whatever is wasted
options.rationale: Chosen by reading 'step-up' as a boost that creates energy.

mcqs.stem: A transmission cable has a resistance of 4.0 Ω and carries a current of 100 A. What power is wasted heating the cable?

options.rationale: 100 × 4.0, from dropping the square; this is the potential difference in volts.
100 × 4.0², from squaring the resistance instead of the current.
100² × 4.0² , from squaring both quantities in the equation.

mcqs.stem: The same electrical power is transmitted at ten times the potential difference, so the current in the cables falls to one tenth. What happens to the power wasted in the cables?

options.text: It falls to one tenth
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming wasted power is proportional to current rather than to its square.

options.text: It falls to one hundredth
options.rationale: P = I² R and the resistance is unchanged, so scaling the current by 1/10 scales the wasted power by (1/10)² = 1/100.

options.text: It falls to a thousandth
options.rationale: Chosen by cubing rather than squaring the scaling factor.

options.text: It remains unchanged
options.rationale: Chosen by thinking only the cable resistance, which is unchanged, controls the waste.

mcqs.stem: A motor connected to a 12 V supply transfers 18 000 J of energy in 60 s. What is the current through the motor?

options.rationale: The power of 300 W quoted as a current, from stopping the calculation one step early.
18 000 ÷ 12, from dividing the energy by the pd and never using the time.
12 ÷ 300, from inverting the rearrangement of P = V I.

mcqs.stem: A charge of 45 C flows through a lamp and 540 J of energy is transferred. What is the potential difference across the lamp?

options.rationale: 540 × 45, from multiplying the two given values without rearranging the equation.
45 ÷ 540, from dividing the wrong way round.
540 + 45, from adding the given values when the operation is not recalled.
Rearranging E = Q V gives V = E ÷ Q = 540 ÷ 45 = 12 V.

mcqs.stem: An electric kettle is connected to the ac mains and boils some water. Which statement describes the main energy transfer?

options.text: Energy is transferred electrically into the kettle's kinetic store
options.rationale: Chosen by attaching the motor description to a heating device instead.

options.text: Energy stored chemically in the mains is transferred to the water
options.rationale: Chosen by treating the mains supply as a chemical store like a battery.

options.text: Energy is transferred electrically to the water's thermal store
options.rationale: The mains does electrical work on the heating element, which raises the thermal store of the water.

options.text: Energy is transferred by heating from the mains to the element
options.rationale: Chosen by naming the pathway after the effect; the transfer from the supply is electrical.

mcqs.stem: Which change would exactly double the energy an appliance transfers?

options.text: Double the power and halve the time it is switched on
options.rationale: Chosen by attending only to the doubled power; here the two changes cancel.

options.text: Halve the power and keep the time it is on the same
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming an unchanged time keeps the energy unchanged too.

options.text: Double the power and double the time it is switched on
options.rationale: Chosen by matching the word 'double'; this actually gives four times the energy.

options.text: Keep the power the same and double the time it is on
options.rationale: E = P t, so doubling t with P unchanged doubles the energy transferred.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the National Grid is correct?

options.text: It transfers electrical power from power stations to consumers
options.rationale: The specification states that electrical power is transferred from power stations to consumers using the National Grid.

options.text: It generates the electrical power that consumers use
options.rationale: Chosen by confusing the transfer system with the power stations themselves.

options.text: It stores electrical power until consumers switch things on
options.rationale: Chosen by modelling the cables as a store that is drawn from on demand.

options.text: It changes the ac supply from power stations into a dc supply
options.rationale: Chosen by assuming transformers convert between ac and dc rather than changing potential difference.

mcqs.stem: A hairdryer is rated at 1800 W and runs from a 230 V mains supply. What current does it take, and how much energy does it transfer in 2.0 minutes?

options.rationale: 230 ÷ 1800, from inverting the rearrangement of P = V I.
1800 × 60, from converting only one of the two minutes to seconds.

options.text: 7.8 A and 3600 J
options.rationale: 1800 × 2, from substituting the time in minutes instead of seconds.

mcqs.stem: Which quantity is measured in coulombs?

options.text: The flow of charge past a point
options.rationale: Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C.

options.text: The current in a circuit branch
options.rationale: Current is measured in amperes; amp is acceptable for ampere.

options.text: The energy a device transfers
options.rationale: Energy transferred is measured in joules, J.

options.text: The potential difference of a cell
options.rationale: Potential difference is measured in volts, V.
